holidays.name: National Maple Syrup Day
holidays.description: A sticky-sweet salute to the golden liquid that turns pancakes, waffles, and even bacon into a celebration. Pour it generously and try it on something unexpected, like roasted carrots or coffee.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance, and its creator is unclear. It celebrates the long tradition of tapping maple trees, which Indigenous peoples in northeastern North America began well before European settlers arrived.
holidays.funFact: It takes roughly 40 gallons of maple sap, boiled down, to make just 1 gallon of pure maple syrup.

holidays.name: Saturnalia
holidays.description: The ancient Roman midwinter festival began on this date. It was a rowdy celebration of feasting, gift-giving, gambling, and general merrymaking in honor of the god Saturn. Social rules were turned upside down for the occasion.
holidays.origin: Saturnalia began as a Roman religious festival honoring Saturn, the god of agriculture and time. It started on December 17 and grew into a multi-day party. Over time the celebration stretched to a week.
holidays.funFact: During Saturnalia, masters would sometimes serve their slaves at the table. A 'Lord of Misrule' was often chosen to preside over the silliness. Many of the festival's gift-giving and feasting customs are echoed in modern winter holidays.

holidays.name: Wright Brothers Day
holidays.description: A day for looking skyward and celebrating the moment humans first took powered, controlled flight. Fans of aviation mark it with airfield visits, paper airplane contests, and a little wing-flapping optimism.
holidays.origin: On December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained, controlled, powered airplane flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. In 1959 the U.S. Congress asked for an annual presidential proclamation to commemorate the anniversary.
holidays.funFact: The first flight lasted only 12 seconds and covered about 120 feet. That is shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet.
